label: thm:xu-genuineness
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:xu-genuineness}
Let $\Gamma,\,\Delta$ be torsion-free nonuniform lattices in $\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$.
Every continuous isomorphism $f\,:\,\widehat\Gamma\,\longrightarrow\,\widehat\Delta$
satisfies the following:
\[
 f\ =\ \operatorname{Inn}(h)\circ\widehat\alpha,
 \quad h\ \in \widehat\Delta,
 \quad\alpha\,:\, \Gamma\,\xrightarrow{\,\,\cong\,\,}\, \Delta.
\]
The map $\widehat\alpha$ is induced by the discrete group isomorphism
$\alpha$, and $\operatorname{Inn}(h)(z)\,=\,hzh^{-1}$.

label: thm:one-recovery
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:one-recovery}
Let $\Phi\,:\,\widehat{G_K}\,\longrightarrow\, \widehat{G_L}$ be a continuous isomorphism
for which $\Phi(\mu_K\lambda_K)\,=\,g\mu_L\lambda_Lg^{-1}$.
Then this $g\,\in\, \widehat{G_L}$ satisfies the following:
\[
 \Phi(\mu_K)\ =\ g\mu_Lg^{-1},\quad \Phi(\lambda_K)\ =\ g\lambda_Lg^{-1}.
\]

label: thm:constituents
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:constituents}
Let $K\,=\,K_1\#\cdots\#K_r$ and $L\,=\,L_1\#\cdots\#L_s$ be decompositions
into nontrivial prime knots, with $r\,\ge\,2$. Suppose a continuous
isomorphism $\Phi\,:\,\widehat{G_K}\,\longrightarrow\, \widehat{G_L}$ satisfies, up to
simultaneous conjugacy,
\[
 \Phi(\mu_K)\ =\ \mu_L^\alpha,\quad
 \Phi(\lambda_K)\ =\ \lambda_L^\beta,
 \quad\alpha,\,\beta\ \in\ \widehat{\mathbb Z}^\times.
\]
Then $r\,=\,s$, and there exist a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{1,\,\cdots,\,r\}$
and continuous isomorphisms
$\Phi_i\,:\,\widehat{G_{K_i}}\,\longrightarrow\,\widehat{G_{L_{\sigma(i)}}}$ such that,
up to simultaneous conjugacy for each $i$,
\[
 \Phi_i(\mu_{K_i})\ =\ \mu_{L_{\sigma(i)}}^\alpha,
 \qquad\Phi_i(\lambda_{K_i})\ =\ \lambda_{L_{\sigma(i)}}^\beta.
\]

label: thm:reduced
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:reduced}
For nontrivial knots, a continuous isomorphism
$\Phi\,:\,\widehat{G_K}\,\longrightarrow\,\widehat{G_L}$ satisfying
$\Phi(\mu_K)\,=\,\mu_L$ and $\Phi(\lambda_K)\,=\,\lambda_L^\beta$ up to
simultaneous conjugacy, with $\beta\,\in\,\widehat{\mathbb Z}^\times$, has $\beta\,\in\,\{1,\,-1\}$.

For arbitrary oriented tame knots,
\[
 \mathcal R(K)\ \cong\ \mathcal R(L)
 \]
 if and only if either $K\,\simeq\, L$ or $K\,\simeq\, L^\dagger$.

label: thm:peripheral-completion
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:peripheral-completion}
For a compact orientable $3$-manifold $M$ with incompressible toral
boundary, and a boundary torus $T$, inclusion identifies
$\widehat{\pi_1(T)}$ with $\overline{\pi_1(T)}\,\le\,\widehat{\pi_1(M)}$.
In particular, this closed subgroup is isomorphic to $\widehat{\mathbb Z}^2$.

label: lem:quotient-completion
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:quotient-completion}
For any subset $S\,\subseteq\, G$,
\[
 \widehat{\,G/\langle\!\langle S\rangle\!\rangle_G\,}\ \cong\ \widehat G/
 \overline{\langle\!\langle S\rangle\!\rangle}_{\widehat G}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Homomorphisms from either side to a finite group are exactly homomorphisms from $G$
with $S$ lying in the kernel. Continuity makes the kernel closed, so the completed maps
annihilate the closed normal closure. Their compatible inverse limits agree.
head: environment

label: lem:scalar
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:scalar}
If $a,\,b\,\in\,\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$ and $u\,\in\,\widehat{\mathbb Z}^\times$ satisfy $a\,=\,bu$,
then $a\,=\,\epsilon b$ and $u\,=\,\epsilon$ for $\epsilon\,\in\,\{1,\,-1\}$.
Consequently, if $A,\,B$ are integral matrices with $B\,\ne\,0$ and
$A\,=\,\eta B$, where $\eta\,\in\,\widehat{\mathbb Z}^\times$, then $\eta\,=\,\pm1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
In each $\mathbb Z_p$, the $p$-adic valuations of $a,\,b$ agree because $u$ is a
unit: these valuations are the exponents of $p$ in $|a|,\,|b|$. Unique
factorization gives $|a|\,=\,|b|$. Cancel the nonzero integer
$b$ in $b(u-\epsilon)\,=\,0$. For matrices apply this to a nonzero entry.
head: environment

label: lem:integral-vectors
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:integral-vectors}
If $A\,\in \,M_2(\widehat{\mathbb Z})$ and $C,\,D\,\in\, M_2(\mathbb Z)$, with
$\det C\,\ne\,0$, satisfy $AC\,=\,D$, then $A\,\in \,M_2(\mathbb Z)$. If $A$ is invertible over $\widehat{\mathbb Z}$,
it belongs to $\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb Z)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $d\,=\,\det C$, multiplying by the integral adjugate gives
$dA\,=\,D\operatorname{adj}(C)\,\in\, M_2(\mathbb Z)$. Reduction modulo $|d|$ yields
$\mathbb Z\cap d\widehat{\mathbb Z}\,=\,d\mathbb Z$. Each entry of $dA$ is therefore $d$ times an integer;
injectivity of multiplication by $d$ proves the assertion.
Using \eqref{eq:integral-intersection} invertibility follows.

label: prop:finite
title: Proposition
head: environment

label: eq:epi-recursion
title: Proof
body_md:
Precomposition proves that (i) implies (ii) and (iii). It is clear that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:epi-recursion}
 E_P(Q;\,\mathbf x)\ =\ H_P(Q;\,\mathbf x)
 -\sum_{\substack{S<Q\\x_1,\ldots,x_k\in S}}E_P(S;\,\mathbf x);
\end{equation}
the sum is over actual subgroups, including different embeddings of
isomorphic subgroups. Induction on $|Q|$ recovers the epimorphism counts.
A marked quotient occurs precisely when its epimorphism count is
positive, thus proving that (iii) implies (ii).

Assume that (ii) holds. For each open normal subgroup $U\,\trianglelefteq_o\,R$, the set
$\mathcal E_U$ of marked epimorphisms $P\,\twoheadrightarrow \,R/U$ is finite and nonempty.
In the compact product $\prod_U\mathcal E_U$, impose compatibility after
projection whenever $V\,\subseteq\, U$. These closed conditions have the
finite intersection property: for finitely many indices $U_i$, a
marked epimorphism to $R/\bigcap_iU_i$ satisfies all listed conditions
after projection. Compactness supplies a compatible family and a
continuous marked morphism $f\,:\,P\,\longrightarrow\, R$. Its compact image is closed and
projects onto every finite quotient, so it is all of $R$.
Interchanging $P,R$ gives a marked surjection $g\,:\,R\,\twoheadrightarrow\, P$.

A topologically finitely generated profinite group is Hopfian: every
continuous surjective endomorphism is injective. Indeed, for
$\theta\,:\,P\,\twoheadrightarrow\, P$, pullback permutes the finite set of open normal
subgroups of index at most $n$. Their intersection $U_n$ satisfies
$\theta^{-1}U_n\,=\,U_n$, and hence $\ker\theta\,\subseteq\, U_n$. The intersection
of all $U_n$ is trivial. Apply this to $gf$; injectivity of $gf$ gives
injectivity of $f$. The resulting continuous bijection is a
homeomorphism by compactness, thus proving that (ii) implies (i).

label: lem:fibre-slope
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The root is a torus-knot exterior or cable space. On the boundary around
the knot, a neighbouring regular fibre is a push-off following the knot
once, so its longitude coefficient is $+1$. Its meridian coefficient
is the linking number in this fibre framing. In the fixed cable
convention this is $pq$: linking between two parallel torus levels is
bilinear, with the meridian--meridian and zero-framed
longitude--longitude terms zero and the cross terms $1,\,0$.
Expanding $pm+q\ell$ gives $pq$ (see
\cite[Proposition~3.8]{Budney}). Since $p\,\ne\,0$ and $|q|\,\ge\,2$ for a cable,
and both absolute values are at least $2$ for a nontrivial torus knot,
we have $|c_K|\,\ge\,2$. Here the fibre slope is computed on the boundary of a neighbourhood of the cable knot. The above fibre-recognition  result shows that its closure is characteristic. The primitive vector $(c_K,\,1)$ in $\widehat{\mathbb Z}^2$ identifies its closure
with $\widehat{\mathbb Z}$.

label: prop:jsj
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:jsj}
Let $M,\,N$ be nontrivial knot exteriors, and let
$f\,:\,\widehat{\pi_1(M)}\,\longrightarrow\,\widehat{\pi_1(N)}$
be a continuous isomorphism carrying the closure of the exterior peripheral subgroup of $M$ to a conjugate of that of $N$. Denote their JSJ trees respectively by $\Gamma_M,\, \Gamma_N$, rooted at the
vertices containing $\partial M,\,\partial N$. For a connected subtree $\Lambda\,\subseteq\,\Gamma_M$, let
$M_\Lambda$ be the union of its vertex pieces, glued along the edges of $\Lambda$.
Then the following three hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The isomorphism $f$ induces an isomorphism of rooted trees
$\theta\,:\,\Gamma_M\,\longrightarrow\,\Gamma_N$ and congruent data
$(\theta,(f_v),\,(f_e),\,(h_{e,v}))$ satisfying \eqref{eq:edge-congruence}.
The vertex correspondence preserves hyperbolic and Seifert
types. Each $f_v$ preserves the full peripheral structure
of its piece, including both boundaries arising from
JSJ tori and any original exterior boundary.

\item For every connected subtree $\Lambda$ with
$\Lambda'\,=\,\theta(\Lambda)$, the restricted congruent data
induce a continuous isomorphism
\[
 f_\Lambda\ :\ \widehat{\pi_1(M_\Lambda})\
 \longrightarrow\ \widehat{\pi_1(N_{\Lambda'})}.
\]
This isomorphism preserves the conjugacy classes of all boundary
subgroups of the block. These boundaries consist of the original
exterior boundary, when the root belongs to $\Lambda$, and the
tori corresponding to edges with exactly one endpoint in
$\Lambda$.

The map $f_\Lambda$ is obtained from the restricted graph data;
it is not asserted to be the literal restriction of $f$ to an
arbitrarily based block subgroup.

\item Let $\Lambda,\,\Upsilon$ be disjoint connected subtrees joined
by an edge $e$. Write
\[
 j_e\ :\ T_{e,\Lambda}\ \longrightarrow\ T_{e,\Upsilon}
\]
for the source gluing map between the two boundary copies
of the corresponding JSJ torus, and write $j'_{\theta(e)}$
for the corresponding target gluing map.
Let $A_{\Lambda,e}$ and $A_{\Upsilon,e}$ be the normalized
boundary maps induced by $f_\Lambda$ and $f_\Upsilon$ respectively.
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:block-boundary-compatibility}
 A_{\Upsilon,e}\circ\widehat{(j_e)_*}\ =\
 \widehat{(j'_{\theta(e)})_*}\circ A_{\Lambda,e}.
\end{equation}
Thus the two maps agree under the source and target
gluing identifications.

If $\Lambda$ contains the root, the normalized boundary
map of $f_\Lambda$ on $\partial M$ coincides with the normalized
boundary map of $f$ on $\partial M$, as a map
\[
 \widehat{\pi_1(\partial M)}\ \longrightarrow\
 \widehat{\pi_1(\partial N)}.
\]
All normalized maps are understood using fixed peripheral
representatives and the associated boundary-group
identifications.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Nontrivial knot exteriors are compact, orientable and
irreducible, with nonempty incompressible toral boundary.
Their JSJ graphs are efficient by
\cite[Proposition~5.2]{Xu25}.
Consequently, vertex and edge completions embed, and the
profinite fundamental group of the completed JSJ graph
identifies with the completion of the manifold group.

By \cite[Theorem~5.5]{Xu25}, the given isomorphism $f$
induces congruent completed graph data preserving the
hyperbolic and Seifert vertex types. The excluded case
of closed $\mathrm{Sol}$-manifolds does not arise here.
Since $f$ preserves the exterior peripheral conjugacy
class, \cite[Lemma~6.8]{Xu25} places the target exterior
boundary in the vertex corresponding to the source root.
Hence $\theta$ preserves the roots.
Moreover, \cite[Corollary~6.11]{Xu25} gives preservation
of the full peripheral structure at every vertex.
This proves~(i).

Restrict the congruent data to $\Lambda$ and $\Lambda'$.
By \cite[Proposition~3.11]{Xu25}, these data induce an
isomorphism of the corresponding profinite fundamental
groups. The connected blocks are themselves irreducible
with incompressible toral boundary, and efficiency
identifies these groups with
$\widehat{\pi_1(M_\Lambda)}$ and
$\widehat{\pi_1(N_{\Lambda'})}$ respectively.

On each vertex, the induced block map agrees with $f_v$
up to conjugation in the target block.
An original exterior boundary is therefore matched by
the vertex peripheral correspondence. A boundary exposed
by cutting an edge leaving $\Lambda$ is matched by
\eqref{eq:edge-congruence}. These account for every
boundary component of $M_\Lambda$, thus proving~(ii).

We next explain the pointwise compatibility.
For an edge $e$ incident to $v$, write
\[
 B_{e,v}\ =\ \widehat{\iota}_{e,v}(\widehat G_e)
 \subseteq\widehat G_v,
\]
and use primed notation for the target.
The congruence identity is
\[
 f_v\widehat{\iota}_{e,v}\ =\
 \operatorname{Inn}(h_{e,v})
 \widehat{\iota}'_{\theta(e),\theta(v)}f_e.
\]
Consequently, the normalized vertex boundary map is
\[
 \left.
 \operatorname{Inn}(h_{e,v}^{-1})f_v
 \right|_{B_{e,v}}\ =\
 \widehat{\iota}'_{\theta(e),\theta(v)}
 f_e\widehat{\iota}_{e,v}^{-1}.
\]
In particular, after identifying either boundary copy
with the abstract edge group, its normalized map is
the same edge isomorphism $f_e$.

The conjugations introduced when passing from $f_v$ to
a block map can be absorbed into the boundary carrying
element. Any two carrying elements differ by an element
of the normalizer of the target boundary subgroup.
By \eqref{eq:normalizer}, that normalizer is the boundary
subgroup itself. Since this group is abelian, the
difference acts trivially by conjugation.
Thus the normalized block boundary map coincides with the
normalized vertex boundary map.
At the two ends of $e$, both these maps are represented
by $f_e$, which proves
\eqref{eq:block-boundary-compatibility}.

Finally, suppose that $\Lambda$ contains the root.
Both the global map $f$ and the block map $f_\Lambda$
agree with the root vertex map up to conjugation in
their respective target groups. Normalize the root
vertex map using a carrying element inside the target
root group, as supplied by
\cite[Lemma~6.8]{Xu25}.
Absorbing the additional conjugations gives this same
normalized boundary map for both $f$ and $f_\Lambda$.
Self-normalization makes it independent of the carrying
choices. Hence the two exterior boundary maps agree
on every element of $\widehat{\pi_1(\partial M)}$.

label: lem:normalization
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:normalization}
In the setting of Proposition~\ref{prop:jsj}, let $V \leq \widehat{\pi_1(M)} \text{ and }\, W \leq \widehat{\pi_1(N)}$ be the completed vertex groups of the root pieces, with representatives chosen to contain the exterior peripheral closures $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Normalize $f$ by one inner automorphism so that $f(P)\,=\,Q$. Then $f(V)\,=\,W$, and its restriction
$\psi\,=\,f\big\vert_V \,: \,V \,\longrightarrow \,W$  is a continuous isomorphism whose boundary restriction is $\psi\vert_P\, = \,f\vert_P$. In particular, if the normalized $f$ preserves
the exact meridian and longitude, so does $\psi$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The JSJ correspondence gives $f\big\vert_V\,=\,\operatorname{Inn}(g)f_v$, where
$f_v\,:\,V\,\longrightarrow\, W$ is an isomorphism and $g\,\in\,\widehat{\pi_1(N)}$.
Using \cite[Lemma~6.8]{Xu25} choose $b\,\in\, W$ with
$\operatorname{Inn}(b)f_v(P)\,=\,Q$. Both $\operatorname{Inn}(g)$ and $\operatorname{Inn}(b)$ carry
$f_v(P)$ onto $Q$, so $gb^{-1}$ normalizes $Q$ in the
target completion. Formula~\eqref{eq:normalizer} gives
$gb^{-1}\,\in\, Q\,\subset\, W$, hence $g\,\in\, W$. Therefore,
$f(V)\,=\,gWg^{-1}\,=\,W$. Moreover, $gb^{-1}$ centralizes $Q$, so
\[
 \operatorname{Inn}(g)f_v\big\vert_P\ =\ \operatorname{Inn}(b)f_v\big\vert_P.
\]
The literal root restriction consequently retains both
individual marks using the same conjugation. If the marks
were initially given up to simultaneous conjugacy, make that
one global conjugation prior to the calculation.

label: lem:coherence
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:coherence}
Let $V_r\,=\,\widehat F_r\times\overline{\langle t\rangle}$
and $V_r'\,=\,\widehat F_r'\times\overline{\langle t'\rangle}$
be composing-space groups, with inner generators
$x_i$ and $y_j$, outer words
$d\,=\,x_1\cdots x_r$ and $d'\,=\,y_1\cdots y_r$, and
normalized maps $\chi,\,\chi'$ as in
\eqref{eq:composing-chi}. Suppose a continuous
isomorphism $\psi\,:\,V_r\,\longrightarrow\, V_r'$ satisfies the following:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\psi(t)\,=\,t'^\alpha$, with $\alpha\,\in\,\widehat{\mathbb Z}^\times$;

\item $\psi$ permutes the conjugacy classes of the inner boundary subgroups;

\item $\chi'\psi\ =\ \alpha\chi$;

\item $\psi(d)$ is conjugate to $d'^\beta$, with $\beta\,\in\,\widehat{\mathbb Z}^\times$.
\end{enumerate}
Then there are a permutation $\sigma$ and elements
$b_i\,\in\, V_r'$ such that
\[
 \psi(x_i)\ =\ b_i y_{\sigma(i)}^\beta b_i^{-1}.
\]
The pair $(t,\,x_i)$ is therefore carried to
$(t'^\alpha,\, y_{\sigma(i)}^\beta)$ with one
common conjugator for each $i$.
head: environment

label: eq:inner-general-form
title: Proof
body_md:
By (ii), choose a permutation $\sigma$ and elements $b_i$ with
\[
 \psi(\overline{P_i})\ =\ b_i\overline{P'_{\sigma(i)}}b_i^{-1}.
\]
This fixes the direction of the conjugation: the normalized
boundary map is $\operatorname{Inn}(b_i^{-1})\psi|_{\overline{P_i}}$.
The target boundary group is abelian and is
freely generated as a $\widehat{\mathbb Z}$-module by $t'$
and $y_{\sigma(i)}$. Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:inner-general-form}
 \psi(x_i)\ =\ b_i t'^{\rho_i} y_{\sigma(i)}^{u_i}b_i^{-1}
 \qquad(\rho_i,\,u_i\ \in\ \widehat{\mathbb Z}).
\end{equation}
The image of $t$ is $t'^\alpha$ and is central,
so after this same carrying conjugation the
boundary map has matrix
\[
 \begin{pmatrix}\alpha&\rho_i\\0&u_i\end{pmatrix}.
\]
It is invertible over $\widehat{\mathbb Z}$, and $\alpha$ is
a unit. Its determinant $\alpha u_i$ is a
unit, so $u_i$ is a unit as well.

Apply $\chi'$ to \eqref{eq:inner-general-form}.
Conjugation disappears under a homomorphism to
an abelian group, and $\chi'(y_j)\,=\,0$. Thus
\[
 \rho_i\ =\ \chi'\psi(x_i)\ =\ \alpha\chi(x_i)\ =\ 0.
\]

Next quotient by the central fibre and abelianize
the free profinite base. Its abelianization is
$\widehat{\mathbb Z}^r$ with basis $[y_1],\,\cdots,\,[y_r]$.
All $b_i$ disappear in this abelianization.
Applying (iv) to the product $d$ yields
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^r u_i[y_{\sigma(i)}]\ =\ \beta\sum_{j=1}^r[y_j].
\]
Independence of the basis vectors gives
$u_i\,=\,\beta$ for every $i$. Finally $t'$ is
central, so each $b_i$ also conjugates
$t'^\alpha$ to itself. The same $b_i$ therefore
works for both members of the ordered pair.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First make the one global conjugation which
turns the two assumed peripheral equalities
into exact equalities. Since $\alpha,\,\beta$
are units, these equalities also identify
the whole exterior peripheral closure.
Proposition~\ref{prop:jsj} gives a rooted
JSJ correspondence.

The source root is the composing space $\mathcal C_r$,
with $r$ child edges and one external boundary.
The target root is Seifert, has the same
boundary count, and has at least two children.
Among the Seifert root types of knot exteriors,
only a composing space has that property.
The target knot is therefore composite, its root is $\mathcal C_s$,
and $s\,=\,r$. This also shows that being composite is detected
in the marked setting. If the source were prime and the target
composite, applying the same reasoning to the inverse would
give a contradiction.
The correspondence permutes the child edges;
call the resulting permutation $\sigma$.

By Lemma~\ref{lem:normalization}, the root
restriction $\psi$ has the exact actions
\[
 \psi(t)\ =\ t'^\alpha,\qquad \psi(d)\ =\ d'^\beta.
\]
It permutes all inner boundary subgroups.
The global completed abelianization satisfies
\eqref{eq:chi-compatible}, because the given
meridian image determines its coefficient.
Restricting that identity to the composing
root gives $\chi'\psi\,=\,\alpha\chi$.
All hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:coherence}
are now verified. Its conclusion gives the
normalized map on every child torus:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:branch-boundary-map}
 t\ \longmapsto\ t'^\alpha,
 \qquad x_i\ \longmapsto\ y_{\sigma(i)}^\beta.
\end{equation}

Remove the root vertex from the JSJ tree.
The component attached at $T_i$ is the full
subtree of $E_{K_i}$, and its corresponding
component is the subtree of $E_{L_{\sigma(i)}}$.
Apply Proposition~\ref{prop:jsj}(ii) to these
connected subtrees. It gives an isomorphism
of their completed fundamental groups.
Part (iii) transfers the normalized boundary
map \eqref{eq:branch-boundary-map} from the
root side to the branch side. Under the
attachment conventions, these two curves
are exactly the meridian and preferred
longitude of the prime summand. This gives
the required $\Phi_i$ with the common
exponents $\alpha,\,\beta$. A carrying
conjugator is used for the entire boundary
torus, so its two equalities are simultaneous.

label: thm:hyp-regular
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:hyp-regular}
For any continuous isomorphism between completions of cusped hyperbolic
piece groups, its normalized cusp maps have matrices $A_i\,=\,\eta B_i$,

label: thm:hyp-integral-regular
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: prop:automatic-regularity
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:automatic-regularity}
Let $\Phi\,:\,\widehat{G_K}\,\longrightarrow\,\widehat{G_L}$ be a continuous isomorphism of
nontrivial knot completions preserving the exterior peripheral subgroup
up to conjugacy. If its normalized exterior map $A_0$ is integral, then
all normalized boundary maps of its JSJ vertex maps are integral.
For the exact ordered marking, $A_0\,=\,I$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Use Proposition~\ref{prop:jsj}. Every hyperbolic boundary map is integral
by Theorem~\ref{thm:hyp-integral-regular}. An integral Seifert boundary
matrix is upper triangular in fibre bases with determinant $\pm1$, so
both diagonal scales are signs.

For an all-Seifert exterior, $A_0$ forces both scaling factors at the root to lie in $\{1,\,-1\}$, and
\eqref{eq:scale-propagation} propagates them through the tree. Otherwise
each maximal Seifert subtree meets a hyperbolic vertex. At such an
interface, source and target gluing matrices $J,\,J'\,\in\,\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb Z)$ give
$A_S\,=\,J'A_HJ^{-1}$, so the Seifert map is integral there. This seeds sign
scales in that subtree, which then propagate.

At a Seifert--Seifert edge the two fibre slopes are independent over
$\mathbb Q$: parallel fibres would join the fibrations, contradicting JSJ
minimality. Let $C,\,C'$ have these two source and target fibre vectors
as columns. The common edge map satisfies
\[
 A_eC\ =\ C'\operatorname{diag}(\epsilon_1,\,\epsilon_2),
 \quad\epsilon_i\ \in\ \{1,\,-1\},\quad\det C\ \ne\ 0.
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:integral-vectors} makes $A_e$ integral and hence an element
of $\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb Z)$. This controls its shear entries as well as scales,
consistent with \cite[Lemma~9.3(4)]{Xu25}. All other edges have a
hyperbolic endpoint and integral gluing matrices. The only remaining
piece boundary is the exterior torus with map $A_0$.

label: thm:xu-boundary
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:xu-boundary}
Let $X,\,Y$ be graph-manifolds with nonempty
incompressible toral boundary, as occur as
Seifert blocks in knot exteriors. Let
$f\,:\,\widehat{\pi_1(X)}\,\longrightarrow\,\widehat{\pi_1(Y)}$ be
a continuous isomorphism preserving the full
peripheral structure. Suppose the normalized
boundary maps of $f$ are unit-regular on
selected components $T_1,\,\cdots,\,T_k$, where
$1\,\leq\, k\,\leq\,\#\partial X$. Then there exist
a unit $\eta\,\in\,\widehat{\mathbb Z}^\times$ and two
homeomorphisms $h_+,\,h_-\,:\,X\,\longrightarrow\, Y$ such that,
on every selected component,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:xu-common-scalar}
 A_i\ =\ \eta B_{+,i}\ =\ -\eta B_{-,i}.
\end{equation}
Here $A_i$ is the prescribed normalized
profinite boundary matrix and $B_{\pm,i}$
is the matrix of $h_\pm$ on that component.
Both homeomorphisms realize the prescribed correspondence of the
selected components. The scalar and the choice of sign are shared
by the entire selected set, not chosen separately for its members.
head: environment

label: prop:graph
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:graph}
Let $X,\,Y$ be graph-manifold blocks as in
Theorem~\ref{thm:xu-boundary}, and let
$f\,:\,\widehat{\pi_1(X)}\to\widehat{\pi_1(Y)}$ be
a continuous isomorphism preserving full
peripheral structure. If its maps on a
nonempty selected set of boundary components
are integral, then one homeomorphism
$h\,:\,X\,\longrightarrow\,
Y$ realizes all these prescribed
boundary maps simultaneously, with
coefficient $1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Integral maps are unit-regular, so apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:xu-boundary}. On one
selected torus, $A_i$ and $B_{+,i}$ both
belong to $\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb Z)$. Lemma~\ref{lem:scalar}
gives $\eta\,=\,\pm1$. If $\eta\,=\,1$, then choose
$h_+$. If $\eta\,=\,-1$, choose $h_-$ so
that $-\eta\,=\,1$. The same choice works
on every selected component because
\eqref{eq:xu-common-scalar} uses a single
scalar and consistent signs.
head: environment

label: lem:hyperbolic
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:hyperbolic}
Let $H,\,H'$ be compact orientable cores obtained by
truncating the cusps of noncompact complete finite-volume hyperbolic
$3$-manifolds. Let
$f\,:\,\widehat{\pi_1(H)}\,\longrightarrow\, \widehat{\pi_1(H')}$ be a continuous isomorphism
preserving full peripheral structure. Then one homeomorphism
$h\,:\,H\,\longrightarrow\, H'$ realizes all normalized boundary maps of $f$
simultaneously. In particular each such map is integral.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The interior groups are torsion-free nonuniform lattices.
Theorem~\ref{thm:xu-genuineness} therefore gives
\[
 f\ =\ \operatorname{Inn}(g)\widehat\alpha,\quad
 \alpha\ :\ \pi_1(H)\ \xrightarrow{\,\,\,\cong\,\,\,}\ \pi_1(H'),\quad
 g\ \in\ \widehat{\pi_1(H')}.
\]
Mostow--Prasad rigidity theorem realizes the one discrete isomorphism $\alpha$ by
an isometry of the complete interiors, up to the basepoint
conjugation. Adjusting the cusp truncations in collars gives one
homeomorphism $h\,:\,H\,\longrightarrow\, H'$. We need to check its boundary maps agree
with the prescribed maps of $f$, not merely that it permutes the
same set of boundary components.

Fix a discrete source cusp group $P\,=\,\pi_1(T)$ and its matched
target cusp group $Q\,=\,\pi_1(T')$. Choose a carrying element $a$ so
that the normalized map is
\[
 f_T\ =\ \operatorname{Inn}(a)f\big\vert_{\overline P}\ :\ \overline P\ \longrightarrow\ \overline Q.
\]
The discrete isomorphism $\alpha$ takes $P$ to a discrete
conjugate of a cusp group. The target is $Q$: after taking
closures its target is conjugate to $\overline Q$ under $f$,
and distinct cusp closures are nonconjugate. Hence choose
$s\,\in\,\pi_1(H')$ with $\alpha(P)\,=\,sQs^{-1}$.

For $p\,\in\,\overline P$ we calculate
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cusp-carrying}
 f_T(p)\ =\ (ags)\bigl(s^{-1}\widehat\alpha(p)s\bigr)(ags)^{-1}.
\end{equation}
Both $f_T(\overline P)$ and
$s^{-1}\widehat\alpha(\overline P)s$ equal $\overline Q$.
Therefore, $ags$ normalizes $\overline Q$. Self-normalization
\eqref{eq:normalizer} puts $ags$ in $\overline Q$, and this
abelian group centralizes itself. Formula~\eqref{eq:cusp-carrying}
reduces to
\[
 f_T(p)\,\ =\,\ s^{-1}\widehat\alpha(p)s.
\]
This is precisely the completed boundary map of $h$ with the
corresponding path to $T'$. Its matrix belongs to $\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb Z)$.

Repeat this normalization for every cusp. The carrying elements
$a,\,s$ can depend on the cusp; $\alpha$ and its homeomorphism $h$
remain the same. Thus all cusp maps are realized by one
homeomorphism of the entire hyperbolic piece.
head: environment

label: lem:gluing
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:gluing}
Homeomorphisms of corresponding hyperbolic pieces and maximal Seifert
blocks that realize the normalized maps on all remaining interfaces
can be adjusted in disjoint boundary collars to glue. Their exterior
boundary action is retained.
head: environment

label: eq:actual-gluing
title: Proof
body_md:
At an interface $j\,:\,T_U\,\longrightarrow\, T_V$, with target gluing $j'$, the required
pointwise equality is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:actual-gluing}
 h_V\big\vert_{T_V}\circ j\ =\ j'\circ h_U|_{T_U}.
\end{equation}
Graph compatibility gives equality of their profinite matrices, hence
of the integral matrices by the injectivity of the map $\mathbb Z\,\longrightarrow\,\widehat{\mathbb Z}$. The two torus
maps are therefore isotopic.

Put $k_0\,=\,h_V\big\vert_{T_V}$ and $k_1\,=\,j'\circ h_U\big\vert_{T_U}\circ j^{-1}$.
The target homeomorphism $\delta\,=\,k_1k_0^{-1}$ is isotopic to the identity map.
Choose $\delta_t$ with $\delta_0\,=\,\delta$, $\delta_1\,=\,\operatorname{id}$. A collar is a
product neighbourhood of a boundary with an interval. On a target
collar $T_{V'}\times[0,\,\varepsilon]$, the map
\[
 (z,\,u)\ \longmapsto\ (\delta_{u/\varepsilon}(z),u)
\]
extends $\delta$ at the boundary and becomes the identity map at the inner
face. Extend by the identity map elsewhere and compose with $h_V$.
Its boundary map is now $k_1$, giving \eqref{eq:actual-gluing}.

Collars at distinct boundary components can be chosen to be disjoint, so
performing these adjustments at every interface preserves previous
agreements. No adjustment is needed at the exterior boundary. The maps
and their inverses descend to the glued manifolds. This is the
coefficient-$1$ gluing mechanism of
\cite[Lemma~6.13(2) and Corollary~6.17(2)]{Xu25}.
head: environment

label: thm:relative
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:relative}
Let $M,\,N$ be exteriors of nontrivial knots, and let
$f\,:\,\widehat{\pi_1(M)}\,\longrightarrow\,\widehat{\pi_1(N)}$ be a continuous isomorphism
preserving the exterior peripheral subgroup up to conjugacy. If its
normalized exterior map is $A_0\,\in\,\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb Z)$, a homeomorphism
$h\,:\,M\,\longrightarrow\, N$ realizes that same boundary map.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Proposition~\ref{prop:jsj} matches the rooted trees, piece types, and
full peripheral structures. Proposition~\ref{prop:automatic-regularity}
makes the required maps integral. If every piece is Seifert, take the
entire exterior as one block and select its boundary. The induced map
is a full peripheral isomorphism, so Proposition~\ref{prop:graph}
realizes $A_0$ directly.

Otherwise, apply Lemma~\ref{lem:hyperbolic} to each hyperbolic piece.
For every maximal Seifert block, restrict the congruent graph data as
in Proposition~\ref{prop:jsj}(ii). This supplies a block completion
isomorphism preserving every boundary. Each block boundary is a
hyperbolic interface or the exterior torus: another Seifert neighbour
would contradict maximality. Its map is integral by
\eqref{eq:interface-integrality} or is $A_0$ by
Proposition~\ref{prop:jsj}(iii). The selected set is nonempty, because a
proper connected subtree has an edge to its complement.

Select all block boundaries. Proposition~\ref{prop:graph} realizes them
by one homeomorphism with coefficient $1$. Thus a single sign choice
controls every interface of that block. The hyperbolic and block maps
are compatible on every remaining cut torus; Lemma~\ref{lem:gluing}
joins them. The exterior boundary lies on a hyperbolic piece or among
a block's selected boundaries, so its action remains $A_0$.
head: environment

label: cor:ordered-recognition
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:ordered-recognition}
For oriented tame knots, $K\,\simeq\, L$ if and only if $\mathcal P(K)\,\cong\,\mathcal P(L)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
An oriented equivalence induces the marked isomorphism. Conversely,
normalize the two marks by one conjugation. If one knot is the unknot,
its longitude is trivial; then \eqref{eq:completed-periphery} implies that the
other is also the unknot. For nontrivial knots the marked exterior map
has matrix $I$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:relative} produces an exterior
homeomorphism with that boundary action.

The determinant $+1$ condition, in consistently signed boundary bases, forces
this homeomorphism to preserve the ambient orientation. Meridian
preservation permits extension over the filling solid torus. The
positive longitude coefficient makes its action on the core generator
of $H_1(\nu K;\,\mathbb Z)$ equal to $+1$, so the knot direction is preserved.
For graph knots the argument uses only graph-block realization and
filling.
head: environment

label: prop:local-boundary-intersections
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:local-boundary-intersections}
Let $V$ be the completion of the group of a JSJ piece of a
nontrivial knot exterior. Let $P_i$ denote its completed
boundary-torus subgroups with chosen representatives. Then
the following two hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item If the piece is hyperbolic, the family $\{P_i\}$ is malnormal:
      $P_i\cap aP_ja^{-1}\,=\,1$ unless $i\,=\,j$ and $a\,\in\, P_i$.
\item If the piece is Seifert, let $Z_V$ be the closure of its
      regular-fibre subgroup. Unless $i\,=\,j$ and $a\,\in \,P_i$,
      \[
       P_i\cap aP_ja^{-1}\,\ =\,\ Z_V.
      \]
      The subgroup $Z_V\,\cong\,\widehat{\mathbb Z}$ is contained in each boundary
      group and is characteristic in $V$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The first assertion is
\cite[Lemma~4.5]{WZGeometries}, also stated as
\cite[Lemma~6.2]{Xu25}.

For the second assertion, the original
Seifert boundary-intersection argument is in
\cite[Section~5]{WZGraph}; the form allowing arbitrary completed
conjugators is \cite[Lemma~6.4]{WilkesGraphI}, restated in
\cite[Lemma~6.4]{Xu25}. Characteristic fibre recognition is
\cite[Theorem~5.5(1)]{WilkesSeifert}, or
\cite[Proposition~8.2(1)]{Xu25}.
All pieces here are major Seifert pieces, so the solid torus,
thickened torus, and twisted Klein-bottle bundle exceptions are
absent. The nonconjugacy and normalizer conventions are explained
in Section~\ref{sec:jsj}.
head: environment

label: lem:word-centralizer
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:word-centralizer}
Let $K$ be a nontrivial oriented tame knot and $n\,\ne\,0$ an integer.
Then
\[
 C_{\widehat{G_K}}(\mu_K\lambda_K^n)\ =\ \overline{P_K}\ \cong\ \widehat{\mathbb Z}^2.
\]
If the JSJ decomposition is nontrivial, this element fixes exactly
the root vertex in the standard profinite JSJ tree.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $P\,=\,\overline{P_K}$, $w\,=\,\mu_K\lambda_K^n$, and let $V$
be the completed root group containing $P$. The element $w$
is nonidentity because its boundary coordinate $(1,\,n)$ is
nonzero. If the root is Seifert, $w$ does not belong to its
fibre closure: this was checked after
Lemma~\ref{lem:fibre-slope}. Explicitly, a composing fibre has
coordinates $(1,\,0)$, while a prime Seifert fibre has
coordinates $(c_K,\,1)$ with $|c_K|\,\ge\,2$; neither can have a
profinite multiple equal to $(1,\,n)$.

Suppose first that the JSJ tree has edges, and let $v$ be the
vertex with stabilizer $V$. Since $w\,\in\, P\,\le\, V$, it fixes $v$.
We show that $w$ cannot fix another vertex $v'\,\ne\, v$.
Suppose otherwise. Since vertex stabilizers are closed,
the closed procyclic group $H\,=\,\overline{\langle w\rangle}$
fixes both $v$ and $v'$.
By \cite[Theorem~4.1.5]{RibesGraphs}, the nonempty
fixed-point set $T^H$ is a profinite subtree.
It therefore contains the minimal profinite subtree
$\Delta$ containing $v$ and $v'$, whose existence follows
from \cite[Proposition~2.4.9]{RibesGraphs}.
Thus $H$ fixes $\Delta$ pointwise.

The edge set of the standard profinite tree is closed,
because it is a finite disjoint union of compact coset
spaces. Hence $E(\Delta)\,=\,E(T)\cap\Delta$ is closed in
$\Delta$. By \cite[Proposition~2.1.6(c)]{RibesGraphs},
the subtree $\Delta$, which contains two distinct
vertices, has an edge adjacent to $v$.
This is the profinite-tree argument used in
\cite[proof of Lemma~6.6]{Xu25}; it does not assume
an ordinary finite edge path between arbitrary
profinite vertices.

Let $e$ be that edge. Its stabilizer is a conjugate, by an element
of $V$, of the completed group of an internal boundary torus of
the root piece. This torus is distinct from the exterior boundary
whose group is $P$. Since $w$ fixes $e$, it belongs to the
intersection of these two boundary groups in $V$.
Proposition~\ref{prop:local-boundary-intersections} makes the
intersection trivial at a hyperbolic root, or the fibre closure
at a Seifert root. Both conclusions contradict the preceding
observations about $w$. Thus $v$ is its unique fixed vertex.

Now let $a\,\in\, C_{\widehat{G_K}}(w)$. The equality $aw\,=\,wa$ implies
that $a$ takes vertices fixed by $w$ to vertices fixed by $w$.
By uniqueness $a$ fixes $v$, so $a\,\in\, V$.
In the case of a single JSJ piece we already have
$V\,=\,\widehat{G_K}$, so the same conclusion holds without the
tree argument.

Since $w\,\in\, P$ and $awa^{-1}\,=\,w$, it lies in
$P\cap aPa^{-1}$. The local intersection proposition forces
$a\,\in\, P$: otherwise the intersection is trivial in the
hyperbolic case, or only the fibre closure in the Seifert case.
Conversely $P$ is abelian and contains $w$, so every element
of $P$ commutes with $w$. This proves the centralizer equality.
head: environment

label: cor:word-peripheral
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:word-peripheral}
For nontrivial knots, if a continuous isomorphism sends
$w_{K,n}$ to a conjugate $g w_{L,n}g^{-1}$, it sends
$\overline{P_K}$ to $g\overline{P_L}g^{-1}$.
After this one conjugation, the rooted JSJ correspondence and
the literal root restriction of
Lemma~\ref{lem:normalization} apply.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
An isomorphism preserves centralizers, and
$C(gwg^{-1})\,=\,gC(w)g^{-1}$. Apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:word-centralizer} in the two groups.
head: environment

label: lem:word-integrality
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:word-integrality}
Let $K,\,L$ be nontrivial oriented tame knots and $n\,\ne\,0$.
Suppose a continuous isomorphism $\Phi :\widehat{G_K}\longrightarrow\widehat{G_L}$ satisfies
$\Phi(w_{K,n})\,=\,w_{L,n}$. Then $\Phi(P_K)=P_L$, and the restriction $\Phi|_{P_K}:P_K\longrightarrow P_L$
has a matrix in $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb Z)$ with respect
to the ordered meridian--longitude bases
$(\mu_K,\lambda_K)$ and $(\mu_L,\lambda_L)$.
head: environment

label: eq:word-boundary-shape
title: Proof
body_md:
Corollary~\ref{cor:word-peripheral} gives
$\Phi(\overline{P_K})\,=\,\overline{P_L}$.
The class of $w_{K,n}$ in the normalized completed
abelianization is $1$. Hence the induced automorphism of
$\widehat{\mathbb Z}$ is multiplication by $1$:
\[
 \widehat\chi_L\Phi\ =\ \widehat\chi_K.
\]
If $A\,\in\,\operatorname{GL}_2(\widehat{\mathbb Z})$ is the boundary matrix, this equality
gives its first row. There exist $\rho\,\in\,\widehat{\mathbb Z}$ and
$\beta\,\in\,\widehat{\mathbb Z}^\times$ with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:word-boundary-shape}
 A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ \rho&\beta\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \Phi(\mu_K)=\mu_L\lambda_L^\rho,\quad
 \Phi(\lambda_K)=\lambda_L^\beta,\quad
 \rho+n\beta=n.
\end{equation}
We now use the root type, which is preserved by the rooted JSJ
correspondence.

\emph{Hyperbolic root.}
The literal root restriction of
Lemma~\ref{lem:normalization} is a continuous isomorphism of
hyperbolic piece completions with boundary map $A$.
The weaker peripheral theorem
Theorem~\ref{thm:hyp-regular} gives
$A\,=\,\eta B$ for $\eta\,\in\,\widehat{\mathbb Z}^\times$ and
$B\,\in\,\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb Z)$.
Let $v\,=\,(1,\,n)^T$. Since $Av\,=\,v$, the first coordinate says
$1\,=\,\eta k$, where $k$ is the integer first coordinate of $Bv$.
Thus $k$ is an integer unit in $\widehat{\mathbb Z}$, so $k\,=\,\pm 1$ and
$\eta\,=\,\pm 1$. It follows that $A\,\in\,\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb Z)$.
The stronger integral theorem
Theorem~\ref{thm:hyp-integral-regular} also gives this directly;
the displayed argument records that the one-mark step needs
only the older unit-regularity input.

\emph{Composing root.}
The target root is also composing. Indeed, such a root has at
least three boundary components, whereas a prime Seifert root
is a torus-knot exterior with one or a cable space with two.
The full peripheral correspondence preserves this number.
The characteristic fibre closures are generated by the two
meridians, so
$\Phi(\mu_K)\,=\,\mu_L^u$ for $u\,\in\,\widehat{\mathbb Z}^\times$.
normalized abelianization gives $u\,=\,1$.
Then \eqref{eq:word-boundary-shape} has $\rho\,=\,0$ and
$n\beta\,=\,n$. Multiplication by the nonzero integer $n$
is injective on $\widehat{\mathbb Z}$, so $\beta\,=\,1$ and $A\,=\,I$.

\emph{Prime Seifert root.}
Both root fibre elements have the coordinates of
Lemma~\ref{lem:fibre-slope}:
\[
 h_K\,=\,\mu_K^{c_K}\lambda_K,\quad
 h_L\,=\,\mu_L^{c_L}\lambda_L,\quad |c_K|,\, |c_L|\,\ge\,2.
\]
The root restriction transports the characteristic fibre closure,
so $\Phi(h_K)\,=\,h_L^u$ with $u\,\in\,\widehat{\mathbb Z}^\times$.
Abelianization yields $c_K\,=\,c_Lu$.
The integral scalar lemma gives $u\,=\,\varepsilon\in\{1,\,-1\}$.
Thus, $A$ sends the two integer vectors
$(1,\,n)^T$ and $(c_K,\,1)^T$ to
$(1,\,n)^T$ and $\varepsilon(c_L,\,1)^T$ respectively.
They are independent over $\mathbb Q$, because
$1-nc_K\,\ne\,0$.
In matrix form,
\[
 A\begin{pmatrix}1&c_K\\n&1\end{pmatrix}
 \ =\
 \begin{pmatrix}1&c_L\\n&1\end{pmatrix}
 \operatorname{diag}(1,\,\varepsilon).
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:integral-vectors} now makes all entries of
$A$ integers. Since $A$ is already invertible over $\widehat{\mathbb Z}$,
it follows from \eqref{eq:integral-intersection} that $A\,\in\,\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb Z)$.
This finishes all cases.
head: environment

label: lem:integral-axes
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:integral-axes}
Let $K,\,L$ be nontrivial knots. Suppose a continuous isomorphism
$f\,:\,\widehat{G_K}\,\longrightarrow\,\widehat{G_L}$ carries the exterior
peripheral closures to one another and has an integral normalized
boundary matrix. After carrying them to the chosen representatives,
\[
 f(\mu_K)\ =\ \mu_L^{\epsilon_\mu},\quad
 f(\lambda_K)\ =\ \lambda_L^{\epsilon_\lambda},
 \quad \epsilon_\mu,\epsilon_\lambda\ \in\ \{1,\,-1\}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
normalize by the common carrying conjugation and write
$A\,=\,\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)
\,\in\,\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb Z)$.
An isomorphism of completed abelianizations is multiplication
by a unit $\alpha$. Compatibility with linking number makes
the first row of $A$ equal to $(\alpha,\,0)$.
Thus, $b\,=\,0$ and $a\,=\,\alpha$ is both an integer and a profinite
unit, so $a\,=\,\pm1$. The determinant condition gives $d\,=\,\pm 1$.
Consequently $f(\lambda_K)\,=\,\lambda_L^d$, and the longitude
axis is already preserved.

The other column is the primitive integer slope
$s\,=\,\mu_L^a\lambda_L^c$.
The source meridian closed normally generates
$\widehat{G_K}$, so its image $s$ closed normally generates
$\widehat{G_L}$. Let $E_L(s)$ denote the closed manifold obtained
by Dehn filling $E_L$ along the unoriented slope of $s$.
The Van Kampen theorem gives
\[
 \pi_1(E_L(s))\ =\
 G_L/\langle\!\langle s\rangle\!\rangle_{G_L}.
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:quotient-completion} therefore gives
\[
 \widehat{\pi_1(E_L(s))}\ \cong\  \widehat{G_L}/
 \overline{\langle\!\langle s\rangle\!\rangle}_{\widehat{G_L}}\ =\ 1.
\]
Fundamental groups of compact $3$-manifolds are residually finite, using
Hempel's residual-finiteness results and geometrization;
see \cite{HempelRF,PerelmanSurgery} and the modern account
\cite{AFW}. Hence $\pi_1(E_L(s))\,=\,1$.
The Poincar\'e conjecture, proved by Perelman
\cite{PerelmanEntropy,PerelmanSurgery,PerelmanExtinction}, implies
$E_L(s)\,\cong\, S^3$.

Gordon--Luecke's filling theorem
\cite[Theorem~2]{GordonLuecke} says that a nontrivial knot
exterior has no nonmeridional Dehn filling homeomorphic to $S^3$.
Thus $s$ is the meridian slope, so $c\,=\,0$.
Its orientation is one of the two possible signs, giving
$f(\mu_K)\,=\,\mu_L^{\pm 1}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Compose the given $\Phi$ with $\operatorname{Inn}(g^{-1})$ once.
The new map sends $w_K$ exactly to $w_L$.

If one knot is the unknot, its completion is the abelian group
$\widehat{\mathbb Z}$. A nontrivial knot cannot have abelian completion:
residual finiteness would make its discrete group abelian,
then its cyclic abelianization would make the group $\mathbb Z$,
contradicting the fact that its embedded boundary group is $\mathbb Z^2$.
Thus, an isomorphism involving the unknot has the unknot on
both sides. Its longitude is $1$ and $w\,=\,\mu$, so the assertion
is immediate.

For nontrivial knots, peripheral recovery is
Corollary~\ref{cor:word-peripheral} with $n\,=\,1$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:word-integrality} makes the normalized boundary
map integral. Lemma~\ref{lem:integral-axes} then gives
\[
 \Phi(\mu_K)\ =\ \mu_L^{\epsilon_\mu},\qquad
 \Phi(\lambda_K)\ =\ \lambda_L^{\epsilon_\lambda}.
\]
The exact word equation is
$\mu_L^{\epsilon_\mu}\lambda_L^{\epsilon_\lambda}
\, =\, \mu_L\lambda_L$.
In the independent coordinates of
$\overline{P_L}\,\cong\,\widehat{\mathbb Z}^2$, it says that
$\epsilon_\mu\,=\,1$ and $\epsilon_\lambda\,=\,1$.
Undoing the one initial inner automorphism gives both original
equalities with the original element $g$.
No new separate conjugators have been introduced.
head: environment

label: cor:other-word
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:other-word}
For any fixed integer $n\,\ne\,0$, a continuous knot-group
completion isomorphism taking $\mu_K\lambda_K^n$ to
$g\mu_L\lambda_L^ng^{-1}$ preserves $\mu_K,\,\lambda_K$
with the same $g$. Consequently, marking $\mu_K\lambda_K^n$
also recognizes oriented tame knots.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The preceding centralizer and integrality lemmas were proved
for this $n$. After applying the axes lemma, the word equation
gives $\epsilon_\mu\,=\,1$ and
$n\epsilon_\lambda\,=\,n$. Injectivity of multiplication by
$n$ on $\widehat{\mathbb Z}$ gives $\epsilon_\lambda\,=\,1$.
The unknot case is unchanged. Apply ordered recognition.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Corollary~\ref{cor:ordered-recognition} gives $(i) \Leftrightarrow (iii)$. Since an ordered marked isomorphism preserves the product and thus gives a one-element marked isomorphism, hence $(iii) \Rightarrow (ii)$. For $(ii) \Rightarrow (iii)$. Theorem~\ref{thm:one-recovery} shows that the single marked element recovers the exact ordered pair, giving $(ii)\Rightarrow(iii)$. Thus $(i)$, $(ii)$, and $(iii)$ are equivalent.
head: environment

label: prop:unit-marking-regularity
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:unit-marking-regularity}
Let $K,\,L$ be nontrivial oriented tame knots. Suppose a continuous
isomorphism $\Phi\,:\,\widehat{G_K}\,\longrightarrow\,\widehat{G_L}$ satisfies, up
to simultaneous conjugacy, the following:
\[
 \Phi(\mu_K)\ =\ \mu_L^\alpha,\quad
 \Phi(\lambda_K)\ =\ \lambda_L^\beta,\quad
 \alpha,\beta\ \in\ \widehat{\mathbb Z}^\times.
\]
Then $\beta\,=\,\epsilon\alpha$ for some $\epsilon\,\in\,\{1,\,-1\}$.
In particular its exterior matrix is unit-regular:
\[
 \operatorname{diag}(\alpha,\,\beta)\ =\ \alpha\operatorname{diag}(1,\,\epsilon).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Normalize the common conjugation. First suppose that $K$ is prime.
Then $L$ is prime, because otherwise Theorem~\ref{thm:constituents}
applied to $\Phi^{-1}$, with exponents
$\alpha^{-1},\,\beta^{-1}$, would make $K$ composite.
Proposition~\ref{prop:jsj} and
Lemma~\ref{lem:normalization} match the root groups while
retaining the specified exterior matrix.

If the root is hyperbolic, note that
Theorem~\ref{thm:hyp-regular} gives the following:
\[
 \operatorname{diag}(\alpha,\,\beta)\ =\ \eta B,\quad
 \eta\ \in\ \widehat{\mathbb Z}^\times,\quad B\ \in\ \operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb Z).
\]
The off-diagonal entries of $B$ vanish, because $\eta$ is a unit.
A diagonal matrix in $\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb Z)$ has both diagonal entries in
$\{1,\,-1\}$. Thus
$\alpha=\eta\epsilon_1$ and $\beta=\eta\epsilon_2$, with
$\epsilon_1,\,\epsilon_2\,\in\,\{1,\,-1\}$, and $\beta/\alpha$ is a sign.

If the root is Seifert, then use Lemma~\ref{lem:fibre-slope}.
The characteristic fibre closures give
$\Phi(h_K)\,=\,h_L^u$ for a unit $u$, with
$h_K\,=\,\mu_K^{c_K}\lambda_K$ and
$h_L\,=\,\mu_L^{c_L}\lambda_L$.
Comparison in the embedded exterior boundary group yields
\[
 c_K\alpha\ =\ c_Lu,\qquad \beta\ =\ u,
 \]
 hence $c_K\,=\,c_L\beta\alpha^{-1}$.
The integers $c_K,\,c_L$ are nonzero. The integral scalar lemma
therefore gives $\beta\alpha^{-1}\,\in\,\{1,\,-1\}$.

If $K$ is composite, Theorem~\ref{thm:constituents} produces
matching prime-factor isomorphisms with the same $\alpha$ and
$\beta$. Apply the prime argument to any factor. The asserted
unit-regular matrix follows immediately.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Apply Proposition~\ref{prop:unit-marking-regularity} with
$\alpha\,=\,1$. It gives $\beta\,=\,\epsilon\alpha\,=\,\epsilon$ with
$\epsilon\in\{1,\,-1\}$. The argument uses only peripheral
regularity, characteristic Seifert fibres, and prime coherence.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathcal R(K)\,\cong\,\mathcal R(L)$. If one knot is the unknot,
its longitude subgroup is trivial, whereas a nontrivial knot
has a nontrivial embedded longitude closure. Both knots are
therefore unknots in that case.

For nontrivial knots the isomorphism sends the longitude
generator to a unit power $\lambda_L^\beta$, using the same
carrying conjugation that identifies the meridians. The first
assertion gives $\beta\,=\,1$ or $\beta\,=\,-1$. If $\beta\,=\,1$,
Theorem~\ref{thm:main} gives $K\,\simeq\, L$. If $\beta\,=\,-1$,
compose with the natural reversed-mirror map for $L$ described
in \eqref{eq:dagger-marks}. It fixes the positive meridian and
inverts the preferred longitude. The composite is consequently
an exact ordered marked isomorphism to $L^\dagger$, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:main} gives $K\,\simeq\, L^\dagger$.

Conversely an oriented equivalence preserves the reduced marking,
and the reversed-mirror map preserves the meridian and the
longitude subgroup. This proves both directions.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Theorem~\ref{thm:main} identifies oriented knot
equivalence with both $\mathcal W(K)\,\cong\,\mathcal W(L)$ and $\mathcal P(K)\,\cong\,\mathcal P(L)$.
Proposition~\ref{prop:finite} with one mark identifies the first
isomorphism with equality of $\mathcal Q_w(K),\,\mathcal Q_w(L)$ and of all counts
$N_Q(z;K),\,N_Q(z;L)$. With two marks it identifies the second
isomorphism with equality of $\mathcal Q(K),\,\mathcal Q(L)$ and of all
meridian--longitude counts. These are exactly the coefficients
of the colouring polynomials by
\eqref{eq:polynomial-coefficient}. This proves all five
equivalences.

label: cor:finite-witness
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:finite-witness}
If oriented knots $K,\,L$ are inequivalent, a finite
quotient with one marked element occurs for one and not the other,
and there are a finite group $F$ and $z\,\in \,F$ such that
$N_F(z;K)\,\ne\, N_F(z;L)$. There is also a finite ordered
peripheral quotient occurring for just one knot, and a finite
group $Q$ and $x\,\in\, Q$ with $P_Q^x(K)\,\ne\, P_Q^x(L)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:main} and
Corollary~\ref{cor:finite-witness-algebraic}.

label: prop:cyclic-lift
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:cyclic-lift}
Let $\rho\,:\,G_K\,\twoheadrightarrow\, F$ be an epimorphism to a finite perfect group.
Put $a\,=\,\rho(\mu_K)$ and $b\,=\,\rho(\lambda_K)$, and let $n$ be a
positive multiple of the order of $a$. Define
\[
 q\ :\ G_K\ \longrightarrow\ F\times C_n,\quad
 g\ \longmapsto\ \bigl(\rho(g),\,z^{\chi_K(g)}\bigr).
\]
Then $q$ is surjective, and
\[
 q(P_K)\ =\ \langle(a,z),(b,1)\rangle
\ \cong\ C_n\times C_{\operatorname{ord}(b)}.
\]
In particular, $|q(P_K)|\,=\,n\,\operatorname{ord}(b)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Both coordinate maps are homomorphisms. Write $H\,=\,q(G_K)$.
Its projection to $F$ is surjective, so its commutator subgroup
projects onto $[F,\,F]\,=\,F$. But every commutator in $F\times C_n$
lies in $F\times\{1\}$. Thus $[H,\,H]\,=\,F\times\{1\}$.
The second projection of $H$ is also surjective because
$\chi_K(\mu_K)\,=\,1$, so $H\,=\,F\times C_n$.

The longitude has $\chi_K$-value zero, giving the displayed
peripheral generators. They commute because the original two
marks commute. The element $(a,\,z)$ has order $n$, and its cyclic
group has trivial intersection with
$\langle(b,\,1)\rangle$: an element of the former with second
coordinate $1$ has exponent divisible by $n$ and is the identity.
The two commuting cyclic groups therefore give their direct
product.

label: thm:granny-square
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:granny-square}
There is a quotient $q\,:\,G_{K_s}\,\twoheadrightarrow\, A_5\times C_5$ whose
peripheral image has order $5$. There is no quotient
$G_{K_g}\twoheadrightarrow A_5\times C_5$ with peripheral image of order $5$.
Thus the sets of finite quotient groups equipped with the image
of the peripheral subgroup distinguish the square and granny knots.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The square witness is any lifted map for which both factors are
full. Suppose a granny epimorphism to $A_5\times C_5$ had
peripheral image of order $5$. Its $A_5$ projection is
surjective, so the meridian image there is nonidentity:
a meridian normally generates the knot group. Its order
divides $5$, hence it is a $5$-cycle. The $C_5$ projection
sends the meridian to a generator, since the map is surjective
and the knot abelianization is generated by that meridian.
Conjugation by a permutation of the five symbols carries any
$5$-cycle to $a$ and is an automorphism of $A_5$; an automorphism
of $C_5$ carries that generator to $z$.

After applying these target automorphisms we are in the normalized
situation of the table. The cyclic component is exactly
$\chi_{K_g}$ modulo $5$, and every full $A_5$ map has longitude
$a^{-1}$ or $a^{-2}$. Its peripheral image therefore has order
$25$, a contradiction. Subgroup order is preserved by every
isomorphism of the finite target, so the distinction does not
require any named generators.
head: environment

label: prop:one-word-A5
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:one-word-A5}
For the oriented granny and square knots fixed above,
\[
 N_{A_5}(1;K_g)\ =\ 241,\qquad N_{A_5}(1;K_s)\ =\ 121.
\]
Among epimorphisms to $A_5$, the respective counts with
$\rho(\mu\lambda)=1$ are $240$ and $120$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix a meridian image $a$ of order $5$.
Multiplying each longitude in the preceding table by $a$
shows that $w$ has image $1$ for $10$ granny maps and $5$
square maps: in the square case only the first-full,
second-cyclic row contributes. These maps are all surjective.
The one additional pair with both factors cyclic has longitude
$1$ and hence word image $a$, not $1$.
There are $24$ elements of order $5$ in $A_5$.
Conjugation by a permutation, possibly odd, induces an
automorphism of $A_5$ carrying any chosen $5$-cycle to $a$,
so the count is the same for all of them. This contributes
$24\cdot10=240$ and $24\cdot5=120$.

We check that the other meridian orders add only the trivial
representation. A meridian image $1$ makes the whole map
trivial by normal generation. Suppose its order is $2$ or $3$
and consider either trefoil factor. Put $h=x^2=y^3$ as above;
it centralizes the meridian image. For an element of order $2$,
its centralizer in $A_5$ is a Klein four group, namely
$C_2\times C_2$, whose nonidentity elements all have order $2$.
But no square in $A_5$ has order $2$, since $A_5$ has no
element of order $4$. Hence $h=1$.
For a meridian of order $3$, its centralizer is its cyclic
group of order $3$. If $h\ne1$, both $x,y$ centralize its
generator and the image is cyclic; otherwise $h=1$ already.
In the cyclic case the preferred longitude is trivial because
it belongs to the commutator subgroup. In the other cases
$\lambda=h\,\mu^{-6}=1$.
Thus both summand longitudes are trivial for these meridian
orders and $w$ has the nonidentity meridian image.
The only remaining contribution to $N_{A_5}(1;-)$ is therefore
the one trivial representation, giving $241$ and $121$.
